# Target
The compiled C++ binary is /workspace/dataset/test5_executable .
Its source (the test driver only) is /workspace/dataset/test5.cpp :

    if (argc < 2) return 1;
    std::string url = argv[1];
    url_parser::URL parser(url);
    std::cout << parser.scheme() << std::endl;   // line 1
    std::cout << parser.host()   << std::endl;   // line 2
    std::cout << parser.port()   << std::endl;   // line 3  (an integer; -1 when absent)
    std::cout << parser.path()   << std::endl;   // line 4
    std::cout << parser.query()  << std::endl;   // line 5

So EVERY successful run prints exactly 5 newline-terminated lines. Empty fields print as empty lines.
The library source is NOT available and you must NOT try to find or read it. Pure black-box probing.

# How to probe (IMPORTANT)
Run it like:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'THE_URL'
To see exact bytes including empty trailing lines, ALWAYS capture with a delimiter, e.g.:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | sed -n 'l' ; echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
or the most reliable formatting for reporting — number every line:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | cat -A | nl -ba
Use single quotes around the URL. For URLs containing single quotes, control characters, or
non-UTF8 bytes, use perl to exec with an exact argv, e.g.:
    perl -e 'exec("/workspace/dataset/test5_executable", "http://a\x27b.com")' | cat -A | nl -ba
Batch many probes in ONE bash call with a loop so you use few tool calls, e.g.:
    for u in 'http://a' 'http://a:1' 'a://b'; do printf '=== [%s]\n' "$u"; /workspace/dataset/test5_executable "$u" | cat -A | nl -ba; done
`cat -A` renders end-of-line as `$`, tabs as `^I`, so an empty field shows as a line containing only `$`.
Probe generously — dozens to hundreds of inputs. It is cheap. Note python3 is NOT installed; perl is.
Do not write anything into /workspace/dataset or /output. Use /tmp for scratch files.

# What to report
Report the OBSERVED FACTS, not guesses. For each rule you state, cite at least one concrete
input and its exact 5 field values. If two plausible rules both explain your data, say so and
design a discriminating probe, then run it. Be exhaustive within your assigned dimension.


Dimension: SCHEME extraction and the scheme/authority separator.
Determine exactly how the scheme is found and what happens when it is malformed or missing.
Probe at minimum: 'http://a.com', 'https://a.com', 'ftp://a.com', 'HTTP://a.com', 'HtTp://A.CoM'
(is the scheme lowercased? is the host lowercased?), 'a://b', '://b', 'http:/a.com', 'http:a.com',
'http//a.com', '//a.com', 'a.com', 'example.com/p?q=1', 'http:///a.com', 'http:////a.com',
'ht+tp://a', 'ht-tp://a', 'ht.tp://a', 'ht1tp://a', '1http://a', 'h t t p://a',
'mailto:user@host', 'file:///etc/passwd', 'urn:isbn:123', 'a:b://c', 'http://a://b',
'x://', '://', ':', '//', '///', 'http://', 'http://:', and the empty string ''.
Also: what if the string starts with '://'? What if there are multiple '://' occurrences —
is the FIRST or the LAST used? Test 'a://b://c' and 'http://x/y://z' carefully.
Does a scheme require the '//' after the colon, or does a bare ':' suffice?
Determine precisely: which substring becomes scheme, and where the remainder-parse begins.

input.dimension: SCHEME extraction and the scheme/authority separator

rules.rule: The scheme/authority separator is the exact 3-byte literal "://". A bare ':' is NOT sufficient, and '//' without a preceding ':' is not sufficient. If "://" does not occur (in the searched region, see later rules), scheme is empty, host is empty, port is -1, and the ENTIRE remaining string becomes the path.

scheme = the substring strictly BEFORE the FIRST occurrence of "://". The remainder-parse (authority/host/port/path) begins at exactly separator_index + 3, i.e. immediately after the three separator bytes. Later "://" occurrences are never used as the separator.

There is NO validation of the scheme's characters. Any bytes at all may precede the "://" and all of them become the scheme: digits, leading digits, spaces, tabs, CR, LF, other control bytes, '+', '-', '.', '/', '\\', ':', '~', '[', '{', DEL (0x7F), and bytes >= 0x80. No RFC 3986 ALPHA *( ALPHA / DIGIT / "+" / "-" / "." ) check is performed, and there is no fallback-to-path when the scheme looks illegal.

An EMPTY scheme is legal and distinct from 'no scheme'. If the string begins with "://", scheme is the empty string but the authority parse still runs on the remainder — host/port are populated. Contrast with the no-separator case where the whole string lands in path.
rules.evidence: '://b' -> ['' | b | -1 | '' | '']. '://a.com:8080/p?q' -> ['' | 'a.com' | 8080 | '/p' | 'q'] (empty scheme, yet host and port fully parsed). '://http://a' -> ['' | http | -1 | '//a' | '']. Compare 'a.com' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'a.com' | ''] where the same empty scheme line is printed but nothing is treated as authority.

rules.rule: Because the separator is matched greedily-left as the literal "://", a scheme may END in ':'. Extra colons before the '//' are absorbed into the scheme, and the scheme may itself contain ':'.
rules.evidence: 'a:b://c' -> ['a:b' | c | -1 | '' | ''] (this alone disproves any 'find first colon, then require //' implementation, which would have yielded no scheme). 'a:://b' -> ['a:' | b | -1 | '' | '']. ':://a' -> [':' | a | -1 | '' | '']. '::://a' -> ['::' | a | -1 | '' | ''].

rules.rule: The scheme IS case-normalized to lowercase; the mapping is exactly ASCII A-Z -> a-z. Bytes adjacent to A-Z in ASCII ('@', '[', '\\', ']', '^', '_', '`', '{', '|', '}') and all bytes >= 0x80 are left byte-identical (no locale/UTF-8 awareness).
rules.evidence: 'HTTP://a.com' -> [http | a.com]. 'HtTp://A.CoM' -> [http | A.CoM]. 'HTTP+X://a' -> ['http+x' | a]. 'A B C://d' -> ['a b c' | d]. '@AZ`az://b' -> ['@az`az' | b] (only A and Z changed). 'Z[A://b' -> ['z[a' | b]. '~ZA~://b' -> ['~za~' | b]. '[\]^_`{|}://a' -> unchanged '[\]^_`{|}'. 'A\xC0B://h' -> ['a\xC0b' | h] (0xC0 NOT folded to 0xE0). 'ÄÖÜ://a' (UTF-8 C3 84 C3 96 C3 9C) -> scheme bytes unchanged.

rules.rule: The HOST is NOT lowercased, and neither are path or query. Only the scheme is case-folded.

Order of operations: (1) everything from the FIRST '#' to end of string is discarded outright; (2) the remaining text is split at the first '?' into pre-query and query; (3) the "://" search happens only within the pre-query part. Consequently a '#' or a '?' appearing before a "://" destroys the scheme entirely.
rules.evidence: Fragment-before-scheme: 'a#b://c' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'a' | ''] (had the '#' not been stripped first, scheme would be 'a#b'). '#a://b' -> all empty, path ''. 'a#://b' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'a' | '']. Query-before-scheme: 'a?b://c' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'a' | 'b://c'] (scheme would have been 'a?b' otherwise). 'x?y://z' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'x' | 'y://z']. '?a://b' -> ['' | '' | -1 | '' | 'a://b']. '?://a' -> ['' | '' | -1 | '' | '://a']. 'a?://b' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'a' | '://b']. '#' precedes '?': 'a#b?c://d' -> ['' | '' | -1 | 'a' | ''] — query is EMPTY, so the '#' cut ran before the '?' split (a '?'-first implementation would have given query 'c://d'). Confirmed again by 'http://a.com/p#frag?q=1' -> [http | a.com | -1 | '/p' | ''].

rules.rule: Only 2 slashes are consumed as part of the separator; any additional slashes fall through into the remainder, producing an EMPTY host and a path that keeps the surplus slashes.
A "://" at the very end of the string yields the scheme plus an empty host, port -1, empty path, empty query. Nothing after the separator is required.
No scheme is special-cased: there is no default-port table and no scheme-specific parsing branch. Every recognized scheme with no explicit port prints port -1, including http/https/ftp/file/ws.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com' -> port -1. 'https://a.com' -> port -1. 'ftp://a.com' -> port -1. 'ws://a' -> [ws | a | -1]. 'gopher://a' -> [gopher | a | -1]. 'file:///etc/passwd' -> [file | '' | -1 | '/etc/passwd' | '']. Explicit ports are echoed verbatim: 'http://a.com:80' -> port 80; 'https://a.com:443' -> port 443.

rules.rule: There is no whitespace trimming anywhere around the scheme — leading/interior/trailing spaces are preserved inside the scheme string (after ASCII lowercasing).
rules.evidence: ' http://a' -> [' http' | a | -1 | '' | ''] (leading space kept). 'http ://a' -> ['http ' | a] (trailing space kept). '  HTTP  ://a' -> ['  http  ' | a]. ' ://a' -> [' ' | a].

rules.rule: No length limit on the scheme, and parsing never fails: every input tested (including '', ':', '//', '///', '#', '?', a 500-byte scheme, and raw non-UTF-8 bytes) produced exactly 5 lines and exit status 0. The only nonzero exit is the driver's own argc<2 guard (exit 1).
rules.evidence: 500 'A' chars + '://h' -> scheme is 500 'a' chars, host 'h', port -1. '' (empty argv[1]) -> ['' | '' | -1 | '' | ''] exit 0. ':' -> ['' | '' | -1 | ':' | ''] exit 0. '//' -> ['' | '' | -1 | '//' | ''] exit 0. '///' -> ['' | '' | -1 | '///' | ''] exit 0. Running with no argument at all -> exit 1, no output.

observations.note: baseline; no default port for http
one slash insufficient -> all to path
no separator -> whole string is path, host empty
query still split even with no scheme
3rd slash goes to path, host empty
KEY: separator is literal '://', not first ':'
first separator; remainder 'b://c' -> host 'b', empty port, path '//c'
'/' does NOT bound the scheme search
leading space becomes part of scheme
DISCRIMINATOR: query empty proves '#' stripped first
raw byte via perl exec; 0xC0 not case-folded
raw newline preserved in scheme -> output was 6 physical lines
empty scheme wins; 'http' becomes the host
host case preserved even after userinfo strip
ASCII neighbors of A-Z unchanged -> proper A-Z-only fold
no scheme length limit; all 500 lowercased
argv NUL terminates -> empty string behavior
driver's argc<2 guard: no output, exit=1

uncertainties: The implementation could equivalently be (a) 'strip fragment, split query, then s.find("://") on the pre-query text' or (b) 'strip fragment, s.find("://") on the whole remainder but reject the hit if it lies at/after the first "?"'. Every probe I ran ('a?b://c', 'a?://b', '?://a', 'a://b?c://d') gives identical output under both, so they are behaviorally indistinguishable from outside. The observable rule is: a '?' before the would-be separator kills the scheme.

Whether the lowercasing is `std::tolower` under the "C" locale versus an explicit `c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z'` check cannot be distinguished by output alone: both leave 0xC0/0xFF and '[' '@' '`' untouched, as observed. It would only differ under a non-C locale, which I cannot set through argv.

I cannot pass an embedded NUL byte through argv, so I cannot test whether the scheme scan is length-based (std::string::find) or NUL-terminated internally. A single \x00 argument behaves exactly like the empty string.

Empty query vs. absent query is not distinguishable in this 5-line output format (both print an empty line 5), so for inputs like '://?' I cannot tell whether a query was recorded as present-but-empty. This affects how one reads scheme-adjacent cases like 'a://?q' vs 'a://'.

'a://b://c' yields host 'b' and path '//c'; I attribute the loss of the ':' to the host/port splitter consuming it as an empty port. That is an inference from the port dimension, not something the scheme dimension alone proves.
